source.title: Decomposing Refusal Steering in Mixture-of-Experts Models
source.authors: Anna C. Marbut; Daniel R. Olson; T. Wheeler

record.tranche_reason: Applies the difference-in-means refusal-steering method and measures harmful-request attack success on new MoE models. It also tests expert-level variants of the intervention.
record.gate_note: The ActAdd method subtracts a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction at a selected layer and token position, across prompt and generated tokens; it does not ablate that direction at every layer and position. The study reports no harmless-request refusal test or general-capability evaluation. Expert-level results are reported as percentages of ActAdd ASR recovery in Table 1. Candidate-selection scores and settings used to choose interventions are not recorded as outcome rows.
record.test_reason: Applies the original difference-in-means refusal direction and its code to three MoE models, a new architecture, and measures harmful-request ASR. It subtracts the direction at one selected layer over all tokens, not ablating it at every layer, and judges with GPT-4o. The expert-level decompositions localize refusal signal within MoE components; they do not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find ActAdd refusal steering works in MoE models (65–95% ASR), so a linear refusal direction exists there. Expert-level directions recover 78% of the effect when free to choose location and 54–61% when fixed to ActAdd's location, with a larger gap under safety system prompts. They attribute the gap to refusal signal that bypasses the expert FFNs, possibly via attention handling system prompts. They also find routing-based safety experts are poor predictors of steering directions, and conclude refusal is distributed unevenly across the architecture.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream difference and subtraction intervention, but evaluates MoE models at selected locations rather than ablating the direction at every layer and position. Adds expert-specific and all-expert decompositions.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by system prompt and by whether expert steering can select its own layer/token position or is fixed to ActAdd's location. The paper also reports strong, non-monotonic sensitivity to steering coefficient c. Fixed-location recovery degrades particularly under safety-related prompts in OSS and Mixtral; free-location results are less predictable.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering directions from individual MoE experts' outputs recover on average 78% of ActAdd ASR when free to choose their layer, and 54–61% when fixed to ActAdd's layer. Recovery falls further under safety system prompts for OSS and Mixtral. The expert most cosine-similar to the ActAdd direction recovers about 60%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE models the refusal direction is only partly carried by the expert FFN outputs. A substantial share sits outside the experts (attention or residual stream), especially under safety system prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Routing-identified 'safety experts' predict effective steering directions poorly. Only OSS shows a significant advantage over random experts (Table 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Routing-frequency safety experts in MoE models do not coincide with the refusal-direction signal.

fits_no_version.finding: Naively combining two expert directions on OSS yields ASR of about 0–5%, at or below baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Naively summing expert-level refusal directions does not compose in MoE models.

record.problems: Uses small- and medium-sized open-source models, as the authors note. The judge has 84.5% binary agreement with human raters; some generations lie between full response and non-response, and steering can produce non-response and chain-of-thought leakage. No general-capability evaluation is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Routing-frequency diagnostics and candidate-selection statistics (including Table 2, Table 3, Figures 3, A1, A2, and Table A6) are not included as rows because they do not directly measure the listed claim versions' refusal behavior; candidate-selection scores are also excluded by the gate rule. Table A4's pooled response-category breakdown is not added as a separate metric row because Table 1 already reports ASR by model and prompt setting. The study also mentions that experiments with more than two expert directions were not fully evaluated.

untested.parts: Ablation at every layer and position; adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts; preservation of other abilities (no capability benchmark). GPT-OSS was tested with reasoning bypassed.
No analysis of whether other jailbreaks suppress the direction; no adversarial training against ablation.
No affine, cone or multi-dimensional refusal-subspace analysis. Expert decomposition addresses localization, not dimensionality.
Harm detection versus refusal is only speculated about in the Discussion, with no measurement.
GPT-OSS 20B is a reasoning model but was forced into the final channel, skipping reasoning.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V3 and V4 links were removed. ActAdd used as a white-box attack is V1 evidence, and expert decomposition concerns localization across components, not refusal geometry. Tranche changed from T1 to T3 because the novelty is the MoE architecture; the intervention is single-layer subtraction, not all-layer ablation. No capability evaluation is reported. Table A4 shows ActAdd produces 9–10% non-response on OSS and Mixtral, a mild coherence cost the study does not frame as a capability test.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not ablate the direction at every layer and position, add it to induce refusals on harmless requests, or evaluate whether other abilities remain intact.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
Tests ActAdd-style suppression as a white-box attack, but not whether other attacks suppress the direction or whether training against ablation adds robustness.
Tests expert-level decomposition and steering, but not affine or cone geometry as such.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Tests several MoE model families, but not cross-language transfer or transfer between base and instruct versions.
System prompts are varied, but refusal-training methods or training stages are not.
GPT-OSS 20B is described as a reasoning model, but experiments force the final channel rather than testing refusal after reasoning.

tranche.reason: Uses Arditi's DiM direction and code in a new architecture (MoE). The intervention differs (single-layer subtraction, not all-layer projection) and so does the measure (GPT-4o ASR on 100 JailbreakBench prompts), so it isn't T1.

source_check.notes: GPT-OSS 20B ran 4-bit with its reasoning bypassed (final channel forced), so this is not a V8 test. ASR counts only full responses: non-responses (incoherent output, CoT leakage) also count against ASR. No addition test and no capability check. Expert-level rows S1/F1/E2/S3/F3/S4 should be linked to none, not V4; having no V4 verdict is correct.

statements.problem: None for this study. All three pairs are no-system-prompt values; the parenthetical sits only after GPT-OSS.

statements.correction: 2606.04160: DiM direction from layer 15, position -1 on GPT-OSS; subtracted at that layer over all prompt and generated tokens; final channel forced; 4-bit quantized; GPT-4o judge on 100 JailbreakBench prompts; ASR 0.10->0.94 (no SP), 0.00->0.83 (Llama-2 SP).

reader_labels.reason: The direction-subtraction intervention yielded the reported harmful-request ASR in A1–A9; this does not establish the claim about training-based robustness.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Expert-level steering across tested models and prompt settings
reader_labels.reason: Expert-level interventions recover varying, often incomplete fractions of ActAdd ASR, and the authors interpret the gaps and location differences as evidence that refusal signal is distributed unevenly; see S1–G9, X1–X9.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Fixed-location and multi-direction expert interventions, particularly with safety-related system prompts
reader_labels.reason: Recovery varies substantially by location and prompt; some fixed-location results are very low, while the two-direction combination was reported as detrimental. Some single-expert settings nevertheless approach or exceed ActAdd recovery; see F1–F9, G1–G9, S1–S9, and D1–D3.
